scenes.tts: How can an added base regroup every downstream codon? The answer lies in how a cell divides a continuous message. Watch the same ribbon throughout this film. Its letters will stay fixed until we deliberately change them.
scenes.caption: How can an added base regroup every downstream codon? The answer lies in how a cell divides a continuous message. Watch the same ribbon throughout this film. Its letters will stay fixed until we deliberately change them.
scenes.visual: Open on a wide BLUE mRNA ribbon made of large base tiles crossing most of the sixteen-by-nine frame. A GOLD start flag waits near the left edge; later tiles continue beyond the right edge. A TEAL three-slot window hovers above the ribbon and glides without landing. Put the question 'Which groups will the cell read?' above it. Keep a small 'schematic' label at lower right. Tiles drift slowly so the frame never freezes.
scenes.narration: How can an added base regroup every downstream codon? The answer lies in how a cell divides a continuous message. Watch the same ribbon throughout this film. Its letters will stay fixed until we deliberately change them.

scenes.visual: Over the carried BLUE ribbon, show the title 'The Frame Sets the Message' for two seconds. The TEAL window continues gliding and the GOLD start flag shimmers; keep 'schematic' at lower right.

scenes.tts: A ribosome needs a starting place. Once initiation selects that site, a teal reading window locks onto the message. The window covers a triplet, then advances to the next nonoverlapping triplet. Each window position is a codon.
scenes.caption: A ribosome needs a starting place. Once initiation selects that site, a teal reading window locks onto the message. The window covers a triplet, then advances to the next nonoverlapping triplet. Each window position is a codon.
scenes.visual: The GOLD start flag settles onto one BLUE tile. The TEAL three-slot window snaps around the start triplet, pauses, then steps right by one full window width. Each visited triplet rises slightly and receives the label 'codon'. Keep the ribbon continuous and moving gently left under the window.
scenes.narration: A ribosome needs a starting place. Once initiation selects that site, a teal reading window locks onto the message. The window covers a triplet, then advances to the next nonoverlapping triplet. Each window position is a codon.

scenes.tts: The frame is the alignment between that window and the ribbon. Start at a different base, and every box contains different letters. Start at the same base, and the boxes remain fixed as the window moves. A fixed start makes each next triplet a codon.
scenes.caption: The frame is the alignment between that window and the ribbon. Start at a different base, and every box contains different letters. Start at the same base, and the boxes remain fixed as the window moves. A fixed start makes each next triplet a codon.
scenes.visual: Duplicate the same BLUE ribbon into two stacked rows. Place the upper GOLD flag on one base and the lower flag one tile later. TEAL windows march across both rows, producing visibly different triplet groupings. Then fade the lower row to GREY and enlarge the upper alignment. On the rule sentence, lock thin TEAL brackets over every triplet.
scenes.narration: The frame is the alignment between that window and the ribbon. Start at a different base, and every box contains different letters. Start at the same base, and the boxes remain fixed as the window moves. A fixed start makes each next triplet a codon.

scenes.tts: With four bases, singles give four words, and pairs give four times four, or sixteen. Both are fewer than twenty amino acids. Triplets give four times four times four, or sixty-four, which is enough. So fixed-length words must be at least triplets. Only experiments could test the real reading unit.

Triplets give four times four times four, or sixty-four, which is enough. So fixed-length words must be at least triplets. Only experiments could test the real reading unit.
scenes.visual: Transform the carried BLUE base tiles into three on-screen grids labelled 'single', 'pairs', and 'triplets'. Show the capacities as on-screen digits beneath them: 4, 16 and 64, never as molecular structures. The first two grids stay RED and marked 'too few'; the triplet grid turns TEAL and 'enough'. A GREY question mark remains over 'actual unit?' to show arithmetic is not evidence. Place a comparison bar labelled '20 amino acids' beside the three grids, highlighting 4, 4×4 = 16, and 4×4×4 = 64 as each is spoken.
scenes.narration: With four bases, singles give four words, and pairs give four times four, or sixteen. Both are fewer than twenty amino acids. Triplets give four times four times four, or sixty-four, which is enough. So fixed-length words must be at least triplets. Only experiments could test the real reading unit.

scenes.tts: Now replace a base inside a codon. The surrounding boundaries do not move. That codon may keep the same amino acid, specify another amino acid, or become a stop. Later codons keep their original grouping.
scenes.caption: Now replace a base inside a codon. The surrounding boundaries do not move. That codon may keep the same amino acid, specify another amino acid, or become a stop. Later codons keep their original grouping.
scenes.visual: Return to the main BLUE ribbon and locked TEAL brackets. Flip one base tile inside a middle codon, while every bracket stays fixed. Beneath that codon, cycle a GREEN amino-acid block through 'same', 'different', and a RED 'stop' block. Downstream GREEN blocks hold their positions and bob gently.
scenes.narration: Now replace a base inside a codon. The surrounding boundaries do not move. That codon may keep the same amino acid, specify another amino acid, or become a stop. Later codons keep their original grouping.

scenes.tts: Predict what happens if a base is inserted after the start. Will only the nearest codon be regrouped, or will every downstream codon be regrouped? Hold the reading window still and follow the ribbon.
scenes.caption: Predict what happens if a base is inserted after the start. Will only the nearest codon be regrouped, or will every downstream codon be regrouped? Hold the reading window still and follow the ribbon.
scenes.visual: A new blank BLUE tile hovers over an insertion gap just after the GOLD start. Keep the TEAL triplet brackets fixed above the ribbon. Show two large choices: 'nearby only' under one codon and 'all downstream codons' under the downstream ribbon. The question stays centered while the hovering tile pulses.
scenes.narration: Predict what happens if a base is inserted after the start. Will only the nearest codon be regrouped, or will every downstream codon be regrouped? Hold the reading window still and follow the ribbon.

scenes.visual: Deliberate prediction pause. Keep the insertion tile hovering, both answer choices visible, and the question centered. A thin GOLD ring completes one slow turn during the pause; nothing reveals the answer.

scenes.tts: The new base joins the ribbon. Every downstream letter slides relative to the fixed window. New triplets appear all the way along, until a stop ends translation. This is a frameshift: the grouping changed, not merely a letter.
scenes.caption: The new base joins the ribbon. Every downstream letter slides relative to the fixed window. New triplets appear all the way along, until a stop ends translation. This is a frameshift: the grouping changed, not merely a letter.
scenes.visual: Drop the new BLUE tile into the gap. Animate every downstream tile sliding right beneath the stationary TEAL brackets. Replace all downstream GREEN blocks with question marks, then reveal the regrouped GREEN blocks in sequence. A RED stop block appears later and closes the moving window. Label the changed alignment 'frameshift'.
scenes.narration: The new base joins the ribbon. Every downstream letter slides relative to the fixed window. New triplets appear all the way along, until a stop ends translation. This is a frameshift: the grouping changed, not merely a letter.

scenes.tts: Researchers called the shift classes plus and minus. A nearby plus and minus often restored function after a disrupted stretch. Same-sign shifts did not restore the frame until a complete triplet's worth accumulated. The later message then returned to its earlier grouping.
scenes.caption: Researchers called the shift classes plus and minus. A nearby plus and minus often restored function after a disrupted stretch. Same-sign shifts did not restore the frame until a complete triplet's worth accumulated. The later message then returned to its earlier grouping.
scenes.visual: Carry the same ribbon into three stacked trials. In the first, a plus marker inserts a tile and a later minus marker removes one; TEAL brackets realign downstream. In the second, same-sign markers leave brackets displaced. In the third, a complete triplet's worth of same-sign changes restores later alignment. Use no claim labels stronger than 'often restored function in tested combinations'.
scenes.narration: Researchers called the shift classes plus and minus. A nearby plus and minus often restored function after a disrupted stretch. Same-sign shifts did not restore the frame until a complete triplet's worth accumulated. The later message then returned to its earlier grouping.

scenes.tts: In phage experiments, those patterns often restored gene function. They supported a fixed reading point and a triplet, or a multiple.
scenes.caption: In phage experiments, those patterns often restored gene function. They supported a fixed reading point and a triplet, or a multiple.
scenes.visual: Shrink the three trials into a simple evidence board. A GOLD start line stays fixed at left. Downstream brackets on the compensated rows turn TEAL; uncompensated rows remain GREY. Beside the board, grow two cautious labels: 'fixed reading point' and 'triplet or multiple'. Keep 'supported' above them, never 'proved'.
scenes.narration: In phage experiments, those patterns often restored gene function. They supported a fixed reading point and a triplet, or a multiple.

scenes.tts: Genetics supported a fixed frame, but did not assign the dictionary. Cell-free translation and ribosome-binding tests linked defined R N A messages to amino acids. Together, the evidence turned moving boxes into codons with assignments.
scenes.caption: Genetics supported a fixed frame, but did not assign the dictionary. Cell-free translation and ribosome-binding tests linked defined RNA messages to amino acids. Together, the evidence turned moving boxes into codons with assignments.
scenes.visual: The evidence board slides left but remains visible. On the right, a schematic test tube receives a BLUE RNA strip and GREEN amino-acid blocks. It transforms into a simple filter: a TEAL ribosome block stays above while free GREEN blocks pass below. Assigned codons on the ribbon gain GREEN labels. No chemical structures appear.
scenes.narration: Genetics supported a fixed frame, but did not assign the dictionary. Cell-free translation and ribosome-binding tests linked defined RNA messages to amino acids. Together, the evidence turned moving boxes into codons with assignments.

scenes.tts: A substitution can alter a codon without moving later boundaries. An insertion or deletion that is not a multiple of three moves the downstream frame. The lasting lesson is simple. Keep the starting register, and every later codon keeps its place.

scenes.visual: Return to one full-width BLUE ribbon. First flip one tile while TEAL brackets hold. Then insert a tile and let downstream brackets visibly regroup. Reset to the original ribbon, place the GOLD start, and march the TEAL window smoothly across. End with the full frame filled by the ribbon and window, ready to dissolve into the end card.
